The defendant, Jake Williams, 31, a retail store manager, is charged with assault after a fight outside a sports bar at about 11:40 p.m. The complainant suffered a broken nose and needed six stitches above the left eye.

A security camera above the bar entrance shows Jake striking the complainant in the face. The complainant then steps back with both hands lowered, and about two seconds later Jake steps forward and strikes a second time. The camera does not cover the two or three seconds before the first punch, because both people stepped partly out of frame. The bouncer testified that the two had argued inside over a spilled drink and that Jake said "this isn't over" on the way out.

Jake testified that the complainant followed him outside, shouted threats, and shoved him hard against a parked car, that he punched to get free, and that he still felt threatened when he threw the second punch. Responding officers noted no marks on Jake and no damage to the parked car. The complainant testified to being punched without warning while walking to a car.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 26, a bank loan officer, is charged with assault for a beating at a bus stop at around 10:15 p.m. The complainant suffered a fractured wrist and bruised ribs and could not describe the attacker, who wore a dark jacket with the hood up. The attacker took the complainant's phone.

A food truck worker about 15 meters away watched the attack under a streetlight. Four days later, the worker picked Jake out of a six-photo lineup and told the detective, "I'm pretty sure, maybe 80 percent." The next morning, a building manager found the complainant's phone case, with the complainant's ID card still inside, in a trash bin behind the apartment building where Jake lives. The building has 48 units, and the bus stop is about a 12-minute walk away.

Jake testified that he was at home all evening. Phone records show no activity on Jake's phone between 9:40 p.m. and 10:45 p.m. His roommate testified that Jake was home but admitted to falling asleep at around 10:00 p.m.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 38, a city bus driver, is charged with assault after a confrontation in a convenience store parking lot. The complainant suffered a concussion and a cut on the scalp that required staples.

Jake admits pushing the complainant, who fell and hit the curb. He testified that the two had a short argument about a parking space, and that the complainant then grabbed a glass bottle from a trash bin and swung it at his head. Jake said he pushed the complainant away to avoid being hit.

No bottle was recovered, and officers found no broken glass near the spot where the complainant fell. The store clerk testified to glancing at the lot in the reflection of the front window and seeing the complainant "already turning toward their car" when Jake pushed with both hands. The clerk admitted that the glimpse lasted about a second and that posters covered part of the window. The complainant denied picking up anything and said Jake came at them from behind.

Jake called 911 right after the fall and stayed at the scene until police arrived.

The defendant, Ryan Williams, 29, a line cook, is charged with assault after a fight in the kitchen of the restaurant where he worked. The complainant, a coworker, suffered a deep bruise on the forearm and a sprained shoulder.

The complainant testified that Ryan became angry over an order mix-up and struck them twice with a metal ladle. A dishwasher, who is a close friend of the complainant, supported that version. A second cook, who carpools with Ryan, testified that the complainant grabbed Ryan's collar first and that Ryan raised the ladle only to block.

The emergency physician testified that the forearm bruise could come either from a blow or from a defensive block against a held object. The kitchen camera was broken that week.

Text messages show that Ryan wrote to a friend that night: "I lost it at work, I really messed up." Ryan testified that the message referred to yelling during the argument, not to hitting anyone.

The defendant, Brett Johnson, 34, an insurance claims adjuster, is charged with assault after a neighbor was found injured in the shared driveway of a duplex at about 7:00 p.m. The complainant suffered a fractured cheekbone and could not identify the attacker, saying they were struck from behind.

Material under the complainant's fingernails contained Brett's DNA. The two had a long-running dispute about parking, and a third neighbor recorded a phone video at about 1:00 p.m. that day showing the two pushing and grabbing each other for about ten seconds before separating.

Brett testified that he left for a client inspection at 3:00 p.m. and returned after 8:00 p.m. The client confirmed that Brett left the inspection site at about 6:15 p.m.; the drive back takes about 35 minutes. A neighbor across the street testified to seeing Brett's car parked in the driveway "around seven, maybe a little before or after," while taking out the trash, and could not be more precise. A wooden board with traces of the complainant's blood was found by the driveway, without usable fingerprints.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 27, a hotel front desk clerk, is charged with assault after punching a stranger at a late-night food stand. The complainant lost a tooth and suffered a cut lip.

Ryan admits throwing one punch. He testified that the complainant was standing very close to his friend, yelling, and had pulled back a fist, and that he struck first to stop what he believed was an imminent attack on the friend. The friend testified to the same account.

The complainant testified to complaining about the friend cutting in line and said there was no raised fist. The vendor testified that the complainant was "loud and in the friend's face" but could not see the complainant's hands because of the counter. The next morning, the friend texted Ryan: "they were just yelling, you didn't need to swing." At trial, the friend said the message was about a different argument earlier that night, which no one else saw.

A phone video taken by a customer begins just after the punch and shows the complainant on the ground and Ryan stepping back.

The defendant, Brett Williams, 42, a real estate agent, is charged with assault after a former business partner was attacked in a parking garage at 9:20 p.m. The complainant suffered a broken arm.

The complainant testified to recognizing Brett clearly in the garage lights, from about two meters away, and to being hit with a metal pipe. The two had run a small property management business together until it closed eight months earlier, and the complainant was suing Brett over unpaid debts. The garage cameras were not recording that night due to a power issue. No pipe was recovered.

The day before the attack, Brett sent the complainant a text message: "You'll regret this lawsuit." Brett testified that he meant the legal costs the complainant would face, not violence.

A parking attendant saw a person in a gray rain jacket leave the garage on foot right after the attack but did not see the face. Brett owns a gray rain jacket. Brett testified that he was at home alone watching television. His phone shows no activity between 8:00 p.m. and 10:30 p.m., and his home is about 20 minutes from the garage.

The defendant, Brett Johnson, 24, a college student who works part-time at a grocery store, is charged with assault after a house party. The complainant was found in the backyard with bruises on the face and a cracked rib.

At the hospital, the complainant told officers that "the person in the green shirt" pushed them down the back steps and kicked them. Brett was wearing a green shirt that night. Two other guests also wore green, according to party photos. At trial, the complainant said Brett punched them before the fall, a detail not in the first statement. The complainant's blood alcohol level was 0.19.

Another guest testified to seeing Brett and the complainant arguing on the porch, next to the back steps, shortly before the complainant was found. Brett admits the argument, about a borrowed speaker, but says he went back inside and left soon after. A ride-share receipt shows Brett requested a ride three minutes after the time a guest estimated the fall happened, and was picked up at the front door. The guest who found the complainant said the estimate could be off by ten minutes either way.

The defendant, Ryan Williams, 36, a hospital lab technician, is charged with assault after a stranger was beaten on a jogging trail early in the morning. The complainant suffered a fractured jaw and described the attacker only as a person in a gray sweatshirt.

Ryan was stopped near the trail about an hour later, wearing a gray sweatshirt. In a recorded police interview that lasted four hours, Ryan eventually said, "Fine, maybe I hit someone, I don't remember." Medical records show he had taken a prescribed sedative the night before. He had waived the right to a lawyer in writing.

In the interview, Ryan said the fight happened "by the bridge," but the attack took place about 800 meters from the bridge. A trail camera captured a person in a gray sweatshirt running away from the area, but the image is too blurry to show the face.

Ryan testified that he walks the trail daily after night shifts and that he only agreed with the detectives so the interview would end.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 32, an insurance appraiser, is charged with residential burglary of a detached house. While the owners were away for a weekend, someone forced open a rear window and took jewelry, a laptop, and about $800 in cash.

Investigators lifted two fingerprints from the inside surface of the forced window frame, the side facing the room. Both matched Ryan. Fresh pry marks on the outside of the frame matched a flat screwdriver, a common tool. About five weeks earlier, Ryan had inspected storm damage to the rear windows for the owners' insurance company. The inspection report, signed by Ryan, describes an "exterior inspection only."

The owners testified that they did not let anyone into the house during the inspection and did not see the inspector open any window. A fingerprint expert testified that prints on a painted frame can last for weeks and that their age cannot be determined.

Ryan testified that he opened the window from outside to check the seal, which would have meant touching the inner surface, and that he did not record it because it was routine. His roommate confirmed that Ryan was home Saturday evening but away Sunday afternoon, when the neighbors believe the burglary happened.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 34, a hospital pharmacist who works night shifts, is charged with residential burglary after being found at about 3:30 a.m. inside the attached garage of a house two blocks from his own home. Under state law, an attached garage is part of the dwelling.

The homeowner heard noises, looked out, and saw a person with a flashlight working at the side door of the garage for about a minute before stepping inside. The homeowner called 911. Police arrived within six minutes and found Ryan inside the garage, wearing gloves and holding a flashlight, next to a shelf with power tools. Nothing was missing.

Ryan testified that his cat had escaped that evening and that he was searching nearby yards. He said he heard a noise inside the garage, found the side door unlocked, and stepped in to look for the cat. A "lost cat" post from Ryan appeared on a local community app at 1:50 a.m. The cat was found two days later, three streets away.

The homeowner testified that the side door was locked earlier that night. Officers photographed fresh-looking scratches around the latch; a detective said they were consistent with a thin tool. No tool was found on Ryan, and no older photos of the door exist for comparison.

The defendant, Brett Williams, 31, a postal mail carrier, is charged with residential burglary of a house on his delivery route. Someone entered through an unlocked back door during the day and took a tablet, a laptop, and several pieces of jewelry.

A neighbor testified to seeing Brett, whom the neighbor recognized as the regular mail carrier, walking along the side of the house toward the backyard at about 2:00 p.m. Postal scan records show that Brett delivered a package to that house at 1:57 p.m., leaving it at the front door. The postal vehicle's GPS shows him at the next stop four minutes later.

The homeowners left for work at 8:00 a.m. and returned at 6:30 p.m. A different neighbor saw a person in a gray sweatshirt in the backyard "sometime in the afternoon" but could not describe the face.

Brett testified that he walked toward the side gate at 2:00 p.m. only to look for a safer place to leave the package, and that he returned at 4:40 p.m. to eat a late lunch in a shaded spot he often uses.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 36, a freelance photographer, is charged with residential burglary of a house where a glass patio door was smashed and electronics worth about $4,000 were taken.

Police stopped Jake about one kilometer from the house, 50 minutes after a neighbor reported the sound of breaking glass. A lab found three tiny glass fragments on Jake's jacket with the same refractive index as the patio door glass, a type used in millions of doors. Blue fibers on the broken door frame were consistent with Jake's jacket, a mass-produced item.

Jake testified that he spent the evening at a friend's home helping repair a broken window, which explains the glass. The friend confirmed this and showed a receipt for window glass bought that afternoon, but an expert testified that the friend's window used a different type of glass. No stolen items were found on Jake or in his car. Jake has a conviction for burglary from 11 years ago.

The defendant, Brett Johnson, 26, a shift supervisor at a gas station convenience store, is charged with embezzlement of about $6,200 in cash over three months.

The store's records show cash shortages on 13 shifts. Brett supervised 9 of them, and those 9 shortages averaged $620. The 4 shortages on shifts he did not work averaged $150. On Brett's shifts, two cashiers also had access to the registers, but the supervisor was the only person with the code to the safe where cash was dropped.

The camera above the safe shows Brett opening the safe 38 times during those shifts. The video shows him counting cash, but the angle does not show whether any was removed. After Brett was suspended, shortages stopped for six weeks and then occurred twice more, for $90 and $120.

A cashier testified to once seeing Brett put "a folded stack of bills" into a jacket pocket; Brett testified that it was his own tip money from a second job. His bank records show cash deposits of $100 to $200 most weeks during the period, which he says came from weekend work for a wedding photographer; he produced two payment messages from the photographer.

The defendant, Jake Williams, 35, an accounting systems analyst responsible for payroll processing, is charged with embezzlement from a regional trucking company. For 15 months, a person who never worked at the company received biweekly paychecks totaling $41,600, deposited into an account controlled by the company's operations manager.

Jake created the fake employee record and approved each pay run. Jake admits creating the record but testified that the operations manager said the person was a remote dispatcher hired off the books and told him to "just put them in the system." Company policy required payroll staff to verify every new employee with a signed hiring form. No form exists.

An email from Jake to the operations manager, sent a week after the record was created, says: "Make sure the new dispatcher doesn't end up on the org chart." Jake testified that he wrote it because the manager had said the hire was confidential.

The operations manager was also charged and agreed to testify against Jake in exchange for a reduced sentence. The manager testified that Jake came up with the scheme and received $500 in cash from each paycheck. Jake bought a used car with $7,000 in cash during the period; he testified that the money came from savings.

The defendant, Jake Johnson, 43, a facilities coordinator at a commercial property company, is charged with embezzlement for selling the company's surplus office furniture and keeping the money. Jake did not report the income on his tax returns and never mentioned the sales to the current director, who joined two years ago.

The defendant, Ryan Johnson, 25, a graduate student, is charged with leaving the scene of a collision that injured a pedestrian outside a concert venue at about 11:55 p.m. The pedestrian suffered a head injury.

Several people saw Ryan's car pull out of a parking spot quickly and saw the pedestrian fall in the street next to the car. Two witnesses said they saw the car's bumper hit the pedestrian. A third said the pedestrian stepped off the curb, tripped, and fell next to the car without being hit. The pedestrian, who had also been drinking, remembers nothing.

The venue's camera shows the car's brake lights coming on as the pedestrian falls, the car stopping for about two seconds, and then accelerating away. The angle does not show whether the bumper touched the pedestrian. A forensic examination found no damage, fibers, or biological traces on Ryan's car. The emergency physician testified that the injury is consistent with a fall from standing height, with or without being struck.

A breath test three hours later showed a blood alcohol level of 0.05; an expert estimated about 0.09 at the time. Ryan testified that he saw someone fall near the car, thought the person had tripped, and left because he was afraid of being caught driving after drinking.
